title: Obesity Stigma Is a Structural Issue, Not an Attitude Problem
summary: Survey data show obesity stigma is a system design issue. Thomas Tsang, MD, on how between-visit care helps patients speak up and stay engaged.
body_markdown:
October 20, 2026


# Obesity Stigma Is a Structural Issue, Not an Attitude Problem


By


[Thomas Tsang, MD, MPH](https://www.linkedin.com/in/thomas-tsang-md-mph-08b5494)


This edition covers:


- Why patient-reported stigma in obesity care is a signal about system design


- How patient perception impacts care engagement


- What employers, plans, and policymakers can do about it now


In our 2026 survey of more than 3,000 people who used GLP-1s for weight loss, more than


[half of patients reported](https://www.omadahealth.com/resource-center/beyond-stigma-and-scripts-what-the-system-gets-wrong-about-obesity-care)


that their care provider views obesity as a result of their lifestyle choices. Forty-two percent said they've felt blamed for being overweight in a clinical setting, and more than a third reported delaying care because they expected to be judged for their weight.


Weight-biased attitudes among healthcare professionals are well documented and can


[measurably degrade](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/obr.12266)


**** the quality of care patients receive. But I see something else in those survey numbers:


**** it’s not just a matter of unkindness or insensitivity among providers. The majority of my peers, myself included, pursued this profession to help people. These numbers are evidence of a system that doesn't make space for meaningful engagement between patients and providers.


The rise of GLP-1s added a new layer to obesity stigma.


[A study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41366-026-02061-y)


in the International Journal of Obesity gauging laypeople's stigma toward GLP-1 use found that GLP-1 users were evaluated more harshly than people who lost weight through diet and exercise alone, and those who did not lose weight at all. A previous study in the same journal showed more


[negative impressions toward women](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41366-024-01516-4)


who lost weight with these medications compared to diet and exercise.


In June, The Obesity Society (TOS) released a


[policy brief](https://www.obesity.org/tos-releases-policy-brief-help-change-language-obesity/)


promoting more respectful language in describing the condition. "Person with obesity" and "obesity medications" are to be used in place of "anti-obesity medications" as part of its End Weight Stigma campaign, on the grounds that "adversarial terminology can unintentionally reinforce stigma."


Language work and bias training are absolutely necessary in reducing obesity stigma, but those learnings can't be meaningfully applied in sporadic, 15-minute visits and follow-up EHR messages. Change needs to happen at the care level—where and how patients are seen, treated and communicated with.


## The Disconnect in the Exam Room


The American Medical Association


[recognized obesity as a chronic disease](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4988332/)


in 2013. Thirteen years is not long in medicine, and clinical consensus has moved considerably in that window. The cultural narrative around body weight has not; neither patients nor clinicians, while well-intentioned, walk into the exam room completely free of it.


The obesity conversation is complex and nuanced on both sides of the exam room, and short appointments are rarely enough to unpack it.


In the same Omada survey, 61% of patients said they wanted more time to discuss weight loss with their doctor, and 40% said they found it difficult to book an appointment in the first place. Regarding follow-up conversations, 44% said their doctor's practice is too busy to support them between appointments.


When a patient isn't given the time to feel heard, or doesn't feel comfortable expressing certain details, they're not fully engaged in their care plan, and we don't get the information we need to implement it.


The stakes are not marginal. Obesity affects


[40.3% of U.S. adults](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db508.htm)


, and


[real-world data](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2829779)


have shown that roughly half to two-thirds of people who start a GLP-1 stop within the first year. Behind those discontinuations are likely conversations that either didn't happen or happened too late.


### Patient Perception Influences Engagement


Patients' perceptions of their care encounters, regardless of provider intent, impact their engagement and behavior. Survey data showed that 36% of patients said they've delayed making an appointment because of a provider's perceived attitude toward their weight, and 42% reported feeling too embarrassed to ask their provider for a GLP-1 for weight loss.


I've seen this happen in practice. For example, a patient who wants to start medication says she needs to think about it. What she didn't want to admit out loud was her fear of needles. If she'd had the time to feel comfortable enough to express that, she and her physician could have come up with a solution. Another example: a patient stops a medication that was working and doesn't provide a reason; his side effect is too private to raise in a room with a physician he rarely sees.


Perception drives behavior on the provider side too. In one scenario, they may perceive that a patient can't afford an expensive medication like a GLP-1, and decide not to raise the topic. In other cases, a patient may have a


[BMI in the normal range](https://www.thelancet.com/commissions-do/clinical-obesity)


, so the provider may be less inclined to pursue additional cardiometabolic testing. Meanwhile, the patient has a genetic predisposition for—or early markers of— cardiometabolic disease, like high cholesterol or insulin resistance.


When these scenarios happen, the care plan is compromised, and the patient's path to better health is derailed.


## Perception Is Not Provider Intent


Patient perception is real and an important aspect of their care journey. At the same time, that perception isn't always reflective of the provider's intent or attitude.


In the traditional healthcare system, providers are operating under


[countless constraints:](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12372397/)


15-minute visits with competing priorities, mounting administrative tasks and documentation, uncertainty around GLP-1 coverage and prior authorization, and the list goes on.


To paint a picture, a brief visit with a patient who has uncontrolled hypertension, an overdue colonoscopy, and a new mental health concern leaves little room for a meaningful conversation about obesity. In another scenario, a clinician who defaults to lifestyle change rather than prescribing a GLP-1 may be following a coverage requirement rather than stating a belief about the patient's lifestyle. Our own survey bears this out: more than 40% of respondents said their provider required diet and exercise changes before prescribing


**.** When it comes to administrative tasks,


[prior authorization alone](https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf)


consumes roughly 13 hours of physician and staff time per week, and coverage for obesity medication shifts by plan and by year.


None of this is the physician's choice, but rather the system they have to work with. However, it's easy to see how lack of communication can be interpreted by the patient as dismissal or judgment, and make them less likely to engage.


### It's Time to Make Space for the Hard Conversations


We need to stop asking patients to advocate for themselves better or clinicians to try harder.


We are all doing our best with what we've got, it's the system that needs to change. Significant efforts are already being made in this arena:


- Consensus among medical societies that obesity is a chronic disease


- Screening guidelines that put weight and cardiometabolic risk on the primary care agenda


- Language guidelines for clinicians


These are all vital steps toward better obesity care and less stigma, but one major gap remains: better engagement between care providers and patients, so they can have the hard, honest conversations needed to change outcomes.


In the near term, this won't be remedied by longer appointment durations or more frequent phone calls. The provider shortage and an overage of administrative tasks make this impossible. What will make this possible is system-wide adoption of a behavior that society is already fully engaged in: asynchronous communication, i.e. texting and direct messaging, staffed by a care team rather than by the primary care physician's already-full calendar.


Asynchronous contact between in-person visits levels the playing field.


A patient who can't say "I am afraid of needles" across a desk may be more willing to type it in at nine o'clock at night. A patient who won't mention low libido to a physician she just met might be more likely to raise it with a care team member she has been messaging with for six weeks. A patient who stops a medication because of nausea can flag it on day three instead of disclosing it at a follow-up 90 days later, after the therapy has already failed. The disclosure pressure is off when there's no clock in the room.


I’m not describing a chatbot triaging symptoms. This is a job for HIPAA-compliant digital health platforms that enable real care teams and patients to engage with each other, and peel away the onion of their health issues from the ease of their phone. At Omada we call this between-visit care.


This is a change that can be implemented now. Instead of a decades-long process of breaking and rebuilding a highly complex system, it works with the system Omada already has. Busy primary care physicians aren't on the hook for this workstream, it's handled by certified health coaches and clinical care specialists. For patients without connectivity, digital literacy, or a preference for analogue communication, parallel paths are in place.


The technology is ready, the next step is covering this care model at scale.


#### Better Engagement Can Reduce Obesity Stigma


Stigma in medicine exists and deserves continued attention. Treating it as only an attitude problem won't change outcomes, because the barriers to communication and engagement still exist.


Reducing obesity stigma requires us to open up opportunities for conversation, meeting patients where they are, whether it's at home, at work, at the grocery store or on the pickleball court (where you're most likely to find me).


A growing body of evidence links


[engagement to outcomes](https://www.cdc.gov/health-literacy/php/research-summaries/patient-engagement.html)


, and we know that people respond to asynchronous communication in most aspects of their lives. The remaining work is making asynchronous healthcare part of the standard.


Employers, health plans, systems and policymakers all have the power to make asynchronous care models a standard part of obesity care, and healthcare as a whole. Concretely


**:**


- Employers: ask your vendors and carriers what their care looks like between visits, and make between-visit engagement a reported metric in your obesity and GLP-1 programs.


- Health plans: cover and reimburse asynchronous, care-team-delivered support the way you cover an office visit.


- Health systems: staff between-visit care as a defined role with defined scope, so it lands on care teams by design rather than on physicians after hours.


- Policymakers: utilize validated clinical quality measures to evaluate durable outcomes from weight management programs.


Together, we can make healthcare a safer space for everyone.
